25-civ.1: The automobile is idealized as the symbol of American freedom, from Route 66 to the muscle car.
25-civ.2: The Interstate Highway System was built with public money and a gift to the nation.
25-civ.3: Every American city hears "We'll build the train later," and the train is perpetually deferred.
25-civ.4: When a city proposes a car-free zone, the auto and oil lobbies re-engage to pull it back.
25-civ.5: Streets without sidewalks or crosswalks treat the walker and the cyclist as an obstruction.
25-civ.6: "Traffic congestion is caused by too many cars" hides the real cause, a lack of alternatives.
25-civ.7: The population must choose between the damage of car dependency and millions of auto jobs.
25-civ.8: Gas prices spike and crash without pattern, keeping the population grateful when gas is cheap.
25-civ.9: A "reasonable commute" has stretched from thirty minutes to forty-five, sixty, then ninety.
25-civ.10: "Mobility" is applied equally to ride-sharing apps, autonomous vehicles, and sidewalk scooters.
25-civ.11: A civilization built around the automobile tells each person to "reduce your carbon footprint."
25-civ.12: Communities resisting highway expansion through their homes are cast as opposing progress.
25-civ.13: An entire species accepts an hour a day in a sealed metal box as a reasonable arrangement.
25-civ.14: Sealed inside the car, the human cannot feel the rain or smell the soil, and this feels normal.
25-civ.15: The industry pits American auto workers against Chinese auto workers to channel anxiety.
25-civ.16: Film, advertising, and music make the car chase and the road trip into an identity to defend.
25-civ.17: Cities with pedestrian zones are called quaint, and cities with massive transit overcrowded.
25-civ.18: The true cost of automobile dependency has never been comprehensively calculated and published.
25-civ.19: Car dependency is called the people's choice because elected officials passed the highway bill.
25-civ.20: A century of songs, movies, and first cars makes the automobile feel like a relationship.
25-civ.21: "Americans will never give up their cars" is spoken as though it were a law of human nature.
25-civ.22: The highway system is framed as public service, with the slogan "We're keeping you connected."
25-civ.23: The body that walked out of Africa is made to feel it cannot walk to the grocery store.
25-civ.24: In a car culture, the person who walks is marked as poor, eccentric, or idealistic.
25-civ.25: "Progress requires mobility" sounds like wisdom and permits every highway expansion.
25-civ.26: The global automobile economy generates trillions annually, and that size buys political power.
25-civ.27: "The economy needs the auto industry" is the threat used to block the transition away from it.
25-civ.28: Pedestrians, cyclists, and transit riders are discarded by a system that counts only vehicles.
25-civ.29: Walking gave way to riding, rail, and the automobile, and each replacement was called progress.
25-civ.30: Society says "people choose to drive" after a century of engineering removed the alternatives.

26-inst.1: The industry says "therapy is self-care," so engaging with it feels like an act of self-love.
26-inst.2: Employers offer three to six free therapy sessions that work as an onramp to insurance billing.
26-inst.3: The industry keeps faith alive with "better interventions are coming" while outcomes lag.
26-inst.4: Mental Health Awareness Month channels the population's suffering toward professional services.
26-inst.5: Friends and family are devalued with "you need to talk to a professional," not your community.
26-inst.6: Facing rising depression and suicide, the industry prescribes more of what it already sells.
26-inst.7: Therapists must weigh the client's healing against the longer treatment that pays the practice.
26-inst.8: Insurance approves therapy for six weeks, then denies it, then partially approves it on appeal.
26-inst.9: Yesterday's gold-standard treatment becomes outdated, and therapists must pay to retrain.
26-inst.10: Every practice claims to be "evidence-based" and "trauma-informed," and few define either term.
26-inst.11: The industry blames its failures on people who "aren't seeking help early enough."
26-inst.12: Therapists who question the DSM's expansion are labeled "anti-science" and "harmful to people."
26-inst.13: The DSM turns the daydreaming child into ADHD and the worrying adult into GAD.
26-inst.14: A person gets a therapist for trauma, a psychiatrist for medication, and a doctor for the body.
26-inst.15: Rival modalities keep clients cycling between CBT, psychodynamic therapy, and EMDR.
26-inst.16: Social media influencers sell the industry with lines like "everyone should be in therapy."
26-inst.17: Critics of the industry are smeared as "anti-mental-health" and "promoting stigma."
26-inst.18: Requests for treatment outcome data get "outcomes are complex" and "every case is unique."
26-inst.19: The profession treats the DSM's categories as scientific despite pharmaceutical funding.
26-inst.20: Therapists stay in an underpaying system because holding others' pain became their identity.
26-inst.21: The profession says "we treat individuals, not systems," and leaves poverty outside its scope.
26-inst.22: Insurers decide how many therapy sessions are covered and profit when you receive less care.
26-inst.23: The diagnostic system says you need a professional to judge whether their sadness is clinical.
26-inst.24: Therapy-speak like "I was triggered" and "that's my attachment style" becomes the lens.
26-inst.25: "Mental health is health" is true, and it is used to treat all suffering as medical illness.
26-inst.26: Insured clients get limited sessions while clients who pay out-of-pocket get unlimited ones.
26-inst.27: Each DSM edition widens mental illness, so crisis statistics may partly reflect measurement.
26-inst.28: Therapists are burned out and discarded, carrying caseloads that no human can sustain.
26-inst.29: Psychoanalysis gave way to CBT, then DBT, then EMDR, each one generating new training revenue.
26-inst.30: The industry blames a worsening crisis on "insufficient access to services," not its own model.

26-civ.1: The destigmatization of mental health was captured by the industry as a marketing strategy.
26-civ.2: "Therapy is a gift you give yourself" turns being unable to afford it into a character flaw.
26-civ.3: "We're going to solve the mental health crisis" is promised every year as the crisis worsens.
26-civ.4: Every celebrity mental health disclosure pulls the population back into the therapeutic frame.
26-civ.5: A culture that calls grief a disorder teaches the whole population to see itself as sick.
26-civ.6: "You just need to talk to someone" gives a therapist to the person who needs a union organizer.
26-civ.7: Society offers no third option between professional treatment and suffering alone.
26-civ.8: Each mental health breakthrough is hyped as a revolution, then fades into incrementalism.
26-civ.9: Mental health has shifted from "not being sick" to "thriving," a standard almost no one meets.
26-civ.10: "Mental health" covers everything from schizophrenia to stress before a presentation.
26-civ.11: A civilization that produces mental illness tells each person "you have a chemical imbalance."
26-civ.12: Peer support networks are accused of "practicing without a license" and putting people at risk.
26-civ.13: Being "in therapy" has become as routine as the haircut and as essential as the gym membership.
26-civ.14: Friends now say "I'm not qualified to help with this, you should see a professional."
26-civ.15: "Your depression is a chemical imbalance" puts the problem in the brain instead of the economy.
26-civ.16: The education system works as the industry's referral pipeline, from assessment to billing.
26-civ.17: Somatic practices and community care are smeared as "unproven" or "pseudoscience."
26-civ.18: Studies showing modest effects for common therapies are absent from the public conversation.
26-civ.19: Pharmaceutical marketing repeated "depression is a chemical imbalance" until it felt like fact.
26-civ.20: People are bonded to the industry through a cycle of suffering, seeking, relief, and return.
26-civ.21: "Mental health is a personal responsibility" sends people the system made sick back to it.
26-civ.22: The industry tells people "you need professional support" and "self-help is not enough."
26-civ.23: A species that handled grief for two hundred thousand years is told it needs clinical support.
26-civ.24: Therapy language makes every preference a "boundary" and every difficult person a "narcissist."
26-civ.25: "Self-care is radical" turns the inability to change a sick system into a personal practice.
26-civ.26: A multi-hundred-billion-dollar industry is funded by the suffering the civilization produces.
26-civ.27: Phrases like "that's so toxic" and "I'm triggered" turn ordinary friction into clinical events.
26-civ.28: The uninsured, the incarcerated, the homeless, and the undocumented are discarded unseen.
26-civ.29: The asylum gave way to deinstitutionalization, then managed care, each called humane progress.
26-civ.30: "Mental illness is a disease like any other" puts suffering in the brain, not the civilization.

27-inst.1: Drug companies fund medical schools and sponsor conferences until they feel like partners.
27-inst.2: Drug companies give doctors free continuing education that features their own products.
27-inst.3: "The pipeline is full of promising therapies" is printed in every annual report.
27-inst.4: Drug makers win back prescribers by saying "the new version is better."
27-inst.5: Herbal medicine is dismissed as folklore and acupuncture as placebo, so drugs stay first-line.
27-inst.6: The drug industry marketed the "chemical imbalance" theory of depression for decades as fact.
27-inst.7: Doctors prescribe because not prescribing carries the greater malpractice liability.
27-inst.8: FDA approvals arrive unpredictably, driving the industry to make more drugs, not better ones.
27-inst.9: Categories like "pre-diabetes" create new markets by lowering a threshold set by a committee.
27-inst.10: A "statistically significant improvement" may mean two points on a hundred-point scale.
27-inst.11: The company that funded the science says "the science supports our product."
27-inst.12: Scientists who publish critical findings are accused of "cherry-picking data."
27-inst.13: The average American over sixty-five takes five or more drugs never tested in combination.
27-inst.14: Drug makers fund the studies, control the data, and bury unfavorable results.
27-inst.15: Drug makers threaten "if you regulate prices here, we'll invest in research there."
27-inst.16: Patient advocacy groups are funded by the companies that sell the treatments they advocate for.
27-inst.17: Scientists with unfavorable findings face industry-funded counter-research and legal threats.
27-inst.18: Requests for raw clinical trial data are met with proprietary claims and years of delay.
27-inst.19: FDA approval reassures doctors while industry user fees fund most of the drug review budget.
27-inst.20: The medical profession knows its bond with drug makers is compromised but cannot exit it.
27-inst.21: Doctors ask "what else would I prescribe?" because their training skipped the alternatives.
27-inst.22: The FDA decides which substances are legal, influenced by an industry that profits from them.
27-inst.23: The complexity of biostatistics and trial design keeps the public out of drug policy decisions.
27-inst.24: The doctor trained to understand the whole person now functions mainly as a prescriber.
27-inst.25: "We follow the science" shields the industry from asking who funded that science.
27-inst.26: Through funding, education, research, and guidelines, drug makers control the profession.
27-inst.27: Crises like antibiotic resistance justify expedited approvals and reduced regulatory scrutiny.
27-inst.28: Vioxx and Bextra were prescribed, then withdrawn when the liability exceeded the revenue.
27-inst.29: Tricyclics were replaced by SSRIs, then SNRIs, while outcomes did not meaningfully improve.
27-inst.30: The industry that funded the study behind the guideline says "we follow the science."

27-civ.1: The drug industry says "we're saving lives," so buying its product feels like a mission.
27-civ.2: "We developed the COVID vaccine in record speed" is invoked when drug prices are criticized.
27-civ.3: "Precision medicine will transform healthcare" sustains faith in the pharmaceutical model.
27-civ.4: Every pandemic and outbreak pulls the population back to the drug industry through fear.
27-civ.5: The body is framed as a machine that malfunctions, so the fix is always a part to replace.
27-civ.6: "Modern medicine has added decades to lifespan" hides that sanitation and clean water did most.
27-civ.7: Citizens who question drugs are labeled "anti-science," leaving only consumer or denier.
27-civ.8: A cancer drug that extends life by four months is hailed as proof the model works.
27-civ.9: Health now means biomarker targets like LDL below 100, always one number from a prescription.
27-civ.10: "Evidence-based medicine" increasingly means medicine studied by the companies that sell it.
27-civ.11: The industry pricing insulin at $300 a vial blames "the cost of innovation" for a $3 product.
27-civ.12: Anyone who questions vaccine safety is labeled "anti-vaxxer," however valid the concern.
27-civ.13: Millions of children are on stimulants, and the parent who questions it must explain why.
27-civ.14: Regulation recognizes only the patentable molecule, not the plant it was derived from.
27-civ.15: The industry says "without us, the disease wins," so its critics seem to side with disease.
27-civ.16: The media reports drug approvals as breakthroughs, funded by drug industry advertising revenue.
27-civ.17: Every movement that questions drug practices is smeared as "anti-science" without distinction.
27-civ.18: The industry's documented influence on medical guidelines draws no sustained public response.
27-civ.19: Defunding non-drug research made the pill society's default response to any suffering.
27-civ.20: The disease terrifies, the drug promises partial relief, and the relief sustains the faith.
27-civ.21: "There's no cure, only management" is said of chronic conditions that bring recurring revenue.
27-civ.22: The industry says "without us, people would suffer and die," and the feeling prevents scrutiny.
27-civ.23: The human body is treated like a machine that needs chemical maintenance to stay healthy.
27-civ.24: A drug culture leaves the population unable to believe in its own body.
27-civ.25: "Better living through chemistry" says a pill can provide what connection and community should.
27-civ.26: The drug industry's profit margins exceed those of oil, finance, and technology.
27-civ.27: Ads asking "do you have these symptoms?" turn a healthy population's wellness into worry.
27-civ.28: The elderly choose between food and prescriptions, and the market ignores those who cannot pay.
27-civ.29: The era of antibiotics gave way to chronic disease management, then to biologics.
27-civ.30: The word "medicine" shields a commercial enterprise from being evaluated as one.

28-inst.1: Insurers sell slogans like "you're in good hands" that feel like emotional truths, not ads.
28-inst.2: Insurers offer wellness programs because a healthier policyholder is a cheaper policyholder.
28-inst.3: "We're investing in innovation to serve you better" often means more efficient claim denial.
28-inst.4: Insurer donations arrive just as a candidate considers a public option, pulling policy back.
28-inst.5: Insurers set reimbursement rates below the cost of care, so many providers refuse insurance.
28-inst.6: Insurers say "we're making healthcare more affordable" while adding 30% in administrative cost.
28-inst.7: Providers must accept insurers' rates and delays or lose access to most of their patients.
28-inst.8: Reimbursement rates and formularies change unpredictably, keeping providers in chronic anxiety.
28-inst.9: Each policy year, a covered drug moves to a higher tier until the exhausted claimant gives up.
28-inst.10: Insurers deny doctor-ordered care as not "medically necessary," a term the insurer defines.
28-inst.11: Insurers blame high costs on "patients overusing emergency rooms," not their own overhead.
28-inst.12: Reform advocates are accused of "wanting government takeover of healthcare."
28-inst.13: A whole profession, medical billing and coding, exists to translate care into reimbursement.
28-inst.14: Insurers stand between patient and doctor, deciding which doctor you see and what care you get.
28-inst.15: Insurers let employers pick the plan, so employees blame the employer for inadequate coverage.
28-inst.16: Insurance brokers act as advisors to the customer while paid commissions by the insurer.
28-inst.17: Advocates for universal healthcare are smeared as "socialist" in industry-funded political ads.
28-inst.18: Insurers say "we're committed to transparency" while publishing only what regulation requires.
28-inst.19: The ACA's individual mandate compelled the population to become customers of private insurers.
28-inst.20: Practices that rely on insured patients cannot challenge the insurer without risking survival.
28-inst.21: Doctors worn down by prior authorizations learn to complain about the system and comply.
28-inst.22: Insurers say "we negotiate on your behalf" while their protection adds cost and reduces access.
28-inst.23: The complexity of actuarial science keeps the public out of decisions about insurance policy.
28-inst.24: Doctors who trained for a decade now spend more time on insurance paperwork than on patients.
28-inst.25: "Insurance is a partnership" hides that the insurer profits from denying the claims you file.
28-inst.26: Insurers extract about 20% of every premium dollar and decide what care is affordable.
28-inst.27: Insurers warn of a "death spiral" if pre-existing conditions are covered.
28-inst.28: Insurers withdraw from rural areas, so residents travel hundreds of miles for in-network care.
28-inst.29: Indemnity gave way to HMOs, then PPOs, then high-deductible plans, each called innovation.
28-inst.30: Insurers lobbying against universal healthcare say "we support expanding access to coverage."

28-civ.1: Insurance is idealized as one of civilization's great innovations, the pooling of risk.
28-civ.2: Tying health insurance to employment means a worker cannot leave without losing coverage.
28-civ.3: "The market will solve healthcare" has been promised for decades and delivered never.
28-civ.4: Every high-profile accident sells insurance with "see what happens when you're not covered?"
28-civ.5: The uninsured person in the emergency room receives care and a bill that bankrupts them.
28-civ.6: "Insurance provides peace of mind," yet navigating insurance has become its own anxiety.
28-civ.7: The population must fight the insurance lobby for universal healthcare or accept extraction.
28-civ.8: The ACA expanded coverage, the next administration undermined it, and the next restored part.
28-civ.9: High deductibles and narrow networks became standard as "consumer-directed health plans."
28-civ.10: A plan costing $500 a month with a $7,000 deductible is called "affordable coverage."
28-civ.11: Insurers warn "bureaucrats would make medical decisions," as their own bureaucrats already do.
28-civ.12: Nations with universal healthcare and better outcomes are cast as cautionary tales.
28-civ.13: Two-thirds of U.S. bankruptcies are tied to medical costs, and it has become a data point.
28-civ.14: For-profit insurance turns shared vulnerability into an individual risk calculation.
28-civ.15: Insurers warn government healthcare means rationing while they ration through denials.
28-civ.16: Politicians funded by insurers vote against universal healthcare and drug price negotiation.
28-civ.17: Universal healthcare abroad is smeared with "Canadian wait times" and "British rationing."
28-civ.18: Private insurance overhead costs about $500 billion a year and draws no sustained outrage.
28-civ.19: Insurers spent billions blocking single-payer, then called the private system people's choice.
28-civ.20: Stories of the uninsured who lost everything bond the population to the card in the wallet.
28-civ.21: "We'll never get universal healthcare in this country" is said by people never offered a vote.
28-civ.22: The private system is framed as the guardian of choice: "you get to choose your plan."
28-civ.23: A species that survived two hundred thousand years without insurance now feels it can't.
28-civ.24: Health has been redefined as being covered, the card in the wallet, not the body in balance.
28-civ.25: "The free market produces the best outcomes" is believed about healthcare despite the evidence.
28-civ.26: The insurance industry spends $200+ million a year lobbying to block universal healthcare.
28-civ.27: Every pandemic is used to increase enrollment in the current system rather than question it.
28-civ.28: Twenty-seven million uninsured Americans are discarded by a system that cannot include them.
28-civ.29: Employer insurance gave way to the individual market, then the ACA marketplace, each a reform.
28-civ.30: Society calls the choice between inadequate Plan A and unaffordable Plan B a freedom.

29-inst.1: Private prison companies win over depressed rural towns with "we'll bring jobs."
29-inst.2: Prison GED and vocational programs are underfunded and built to produce compliance paperwork.
29-inst.3: "Criminal justice reform is coming" is promised by every administration and deferred.
29-inst.4: Background checks and housing restrictions push released people back toward prison.
29-inst.5: Predictive policing uses biased arrest data to target communities of color, then cites arrests.
29-inst.6: The system says it is "colorblind" while its own data shows every outcome correlates with race.
29-inst.7: Prisoners can accept dehumanization or resist and face solitary confinement.
29-inst.8: A reform bill passes, then a reform is rolled back, preventing sustained progress.
29-inst.9: Mandatory minimums and three-strikes laws extend sentences, and the time is the revenue.
29-inst.10: The system that cages people is called "corrections," though nothing specific is corrected.
29-inst.11: Prisons that offer no reentry support blame recidivism on people who "didn't learn."
29-inst.12: Prison reform groups are accused of "caring more about criminals than victims."
29-inst.13: 1.9 million people in cages is discussed in policy papers like crop yields.
29-inst.14: Solitary confinement holds people, even children, alone twenty-two to twenty-four hours a day.
29-inst.15: Prisons are built in towns that need the jobs, giving those towns an interest in full cells.
29-inst.16: Police, prosecutors, and judges work inside a system that rewards conviction volume.
29-inst.17: Prison reform advocates are smeared as "soft on crime" by the private prison industry.
29-inst.18: Requests for data on prison deaths are refused with "security concerns."
29-inst.19: Voters were never offered rehabilitation on the ballot, yet their votes are cited as consent.
29-inst.20: Correctional officers are bonded to the system through an us-versus-them mentality.
29-inst.21: Prison counselors and chaplains learn the system won't change, so they manage, not transform.
29-inst.22: Reentry initiatives that monitor and track people double as surveillance extensions.
29-inst.23: After years of control, a released person gets a bus ticket and a list of agencies.
29-inst.24: The "ex-con" label replaces the person and is permanent because the record is permanent.
29-inst.25: "They need to take responsibility" is said of the caged person but never of the system.
29-inst.26: Private prison companies spent over $25 million lobbying for the policies that fill their beds.
29-inst.27: Prisons full from sentencing laws cite "overcrowding" to justify building more prisons.
29-inst.28: Correctional officers are used up by trauma and understaffing, then discarded.
29-inst.29: The penitentiary gave way to the reformatory, then the private prison, each called humane.
29-inst.30: The prison company that lobbied for sentencing laws says "we don't make the laws."

29-civ.1: Justice is idealized as the blindfolded goddess with the scales, so questioning it sounds unfair.
29-civ.2: Probation and parole are framed as mercy while extending the system's surveillance and control.
29-civ.3: "Rehabilitation, not incarceration" has been in policy for fifty years as incarceration rose.
29-civ.4: Every media cycle of "rising crime" renews demands for "law and order" and interrupts reform.
29-civ.5: A felon is no longer a voter, an employee, or a tenant in the society that caged them.
29-civ.6: "Land of the free" is spoken by the nation that incarcerates more of its citizens than any other.
29-civ.7: The population can support caging millions or be labeled "soft on crime."
29-civ.8: A viral video or documentary sparks outrage about prisons that fades with the next news cycle.
29-civ.9: The definition of "criminal" expands every decade, so the pool of potential inmates grows.
29-civ.10: "Public safety" justifies every new prison while community investment produces better outcomes.
29-civ.11: A civilization that produced crime through inequality projects the cause onto the individual.
29-civ.12: Communities protesting the policing that fills prisons are called "anti-law-enforcement."
29-civ.13: A nation that incarcerates more of its citizens than any other does not feel it as a crisis.
29-civ.14: Prisons built in rural areas far from urban communities keep society from seeing the cages.
29-civ.15: "Criminals versus citizens" makes the public identify with the system, not the people it cages.
29-civ.16: The media leads the evening news with crime reports and shows the mugshot before the trial.
29-civ.17: Labels like "felon," "offender," and "inmate" replace the person with the act.
29-civ.18: Prison walls hide conditions that would produce public outrage if they were visible.
29-civ.19: Movies and TV present crime as moral failure and punishment as deserved, so no one examines it.
29-civ.20: The crime report activates fear and the arrest brings relief, bonding the public to the system.
29-civ.21: "Some people just can't be helped" is said by a society that never funded the alternative.
29-civ.22: Prisons are framed as "keeping the dangerous off the streets" and "giving them structure."
29-civ.23: Society removes the vote and jury service, saying a person who made a mistake can't be trusted.
29-civ.24: Prisoners are counted in the census where the prison is, not in the communities they came from.
29-civ.25: "We're a nation of second chances" is said by a nation that keeps felony records permanently.
29-civ.26: Public funds that could go to education and housing go to private prison company shareholders.
29-civ.27: The "crime wave" narrative is periodically manufactured to keep public demand for prisons high.
29-civ.28: Whole communities lose members to prison and bear the cost without the promised investment.
29-civ.29: Slavery gave way to convict leasing, Jim Crow, then mass incarceration, each called progress.
29-civ.30: The 13th Amendment abolished slavery "except as a punishment for crime."

30-inst.1: Nations that need labor offer "guest worker programs," a welcome conditional on the labor.
30-inst.2: Foreign aid is conditioned on policy changes that serve the donor nation's interests.
30-inst.3: "Comprehensive immigration reform" is promised by every administration and delivered by none.
30-inst.4: Enforcement is escalated, relaxed, then escalated again, keeping immigrants in uncertainty.
30-inst.5: The label "illegal alien" strips the person whose labor the system depends on of humanity.
30-inst.6: The nation says "we welcome those who come legally" while some legal backlogs are twenty years.
30-inst.7: Undocumented workers must work and risk deportation, or not work and face destitution.
30-inst.8: DACA was announced, rescinded, partially restored, then challenged in court.
30-inst.9: Gang violence that was persecution is now "criminal activity," narrowing who counts as a refugee.
30-inst.10: Politicians who say "we welcome legal immigration" also cut visas and defund the agencies.
30-inst.11: Employers paying below minimum wage say "they're willing to work for less."
30-inst.12: Communities that resist ICE operations are accused of "harboring criminals."
30-inst.13: The detention of children in cages drew national outrage, the outrage faded, and it continues.
30-inst.14: Detention facilities in remote locations cut detainees off from family and legal representation.
30-inst.15: Nations say "we can't take them, let the neighboring country absorb them."
30-inst.16: Immigration attorneys must help clients prove their fear in a format the system accepts.
30-inst.17: Immigrant advocacy organizations are smeared as "open borders activists."
30-inst.18: Requests for detention conditions data are refused in the name of "national security."
30-inst.19: Crimes by immigrants are amplified while crimes against immigrants are ignored.
30-inst.20: Immigration advocates stay in a system that breaks their heart because the work became their identity.
30-inst.21: Advocates fighting the system for decades come to accept its cruelty as the weather.
30-inst.22: Resettlement agencies decide where a refugee lives and what job they take, framed as assistance.
30-inst.23: The nation that extracted the colony's wealth says "they can't govern themselves."
30-inst.24: The child of immigrants belongs to both places and fully to neither.
30-inst.25: "We can't help everyone" is a true statement of capacity that bypasses the moral obligation.
30-inst.26: The detention industry earns billions with the same per diem model as the prison industry.
30-inst.27: "The border is under attack" turns desperate people into a military threat to justify walls.
30-inst.28: Expired applications and families that give up are discarded and no longer counted.
30-inst.29: DACA, the travel ban, and Title 42 each replaced the last while the system stayed unchanged.
30-inst.30: The government that separated families says "we were enforcing the law."
